content:
As part of the DARPA AIQ program I have spent some effort formalizing different theoretical claims, and I've been formalizing results related to a special case of the distributionally robust Schrödinger bridge control problem constructed. Specifically, wrt to DRO theory, the perturbed distribution is bounded by either a Wasserstein or Sinkhorn ball, and the cost is bounded by the DRO dual value. The specific statement is currently niche, but laying the foundations to get there was a significant task.

One example result is a formalization very close to Theorem 1 in
Rui Gao and Anton J. Kleywegt, “Distributionally Robust Stochastic Optimization with Wasserstein Distance,” Mathematics of Operations Research 48(2), 603–655, 2023... The main difference is that it currently has some strong assumptions and is specialized to the quadratic case.

The main repo is here: https://github.com/AIQ-Kitware/aiq-drsb-formalization

It contains a formalization.yaml and challenges for theorems related to Donsker-Varadhan, supergradients, Birkhoff-Hopf, several general KL statements, Wasserstein/Sinkhorn DRO, and there is a roadmap to a more complete stochastic control theory.

Some of the results in this repo are independent proofs of existing work I also found elsewhere:

  • RemyDegenne/brownian-motion was used as a reference for Borel instances on continuous maps.

It also directly vendors portions of code from:

  • RemyDegenne/kolmogorov_extension4 for projective limits.

  • mrdouglasny/gibbs-variational.

There are a lot of directions this formalization could go, my main focus has been the work I posted about in: #AI authored projects > Multidimensional Scaling and Spectral Perturbation PRs but the work here is maturing to the point where its at least worth posting about. I'll likely work on pushing this further, but if there is any particular area that is a more generally interesting target for formalization, let me know and I can spend effort there.

The more I work in this area, the more I'm seeing the need for some centralized location of LLM generated results. Clearly these can't go into mathlib as is, but as the barrier to entry for formalization lowers, it would make the shared task more efficient if it was easier to source other LLM generated proofs that might be relevant. Currently the landscape seems scattered. Wondering what other thoughts on this are.
